excerpt: Section II, The Sampling Theorem (paraphrased for practice), from C. E. Shannon, Communication in the Presence of Noise, 1949. Theorem 1: if a function f(t) contains no frequencies higher than W cycles per second, it is completely determined by giving its ordinates at a series of points spaced 1/(2W) seconds apart. Intuitively, a function limited to the band from 0 to W cannot change to a substantially new value in a time less than one half cycle of its highest frequency, 1/(2W). The function can be reconstructed from its samples by summing sin(πx)/(πx)-type pulses centred on the sample points and weighted by the sample values. The sampling rate 2W is the minimum: samples taken less often than every 1/(2W) seconds do not determine the function uniquely.
focus: Explain the sampling theorem and aliasing with a single sinusoid of frequency f sampled at rate f_s. Let the learner change f and f_s (and optionally the phase). Show the continuous sinusoid, the sample points, and the lowest-frequency sinusoid that passes through the same samples (the alias), with its apparent frequency |f − k·f_s| for the nearest integer k. Guide them through (a) f_s comfortably above 2f, where the alias is the original signal, and (b) f_s below 2f, where a slower sinusoid fits the same samples. Check that the apparent frequency equals f whenever f < f_s/2 and is always between 0 and f_s/2.
audience: Second- or third-year electrical and computer engineering undergraduates who know sinusoids and frequency but have not taken a signal-processing course.
